ABSTRACT
By virtue of its abundant availability, diverse structures, renewability, and cheapness, the rational utilization of 
biomass waste to synthesis porous carbon with a great specific surface area (SSA), high porosity, and superior 
electrochemical capabilities holds substantial significance for energy storage. In this research, waste bamboo 
fibers with a vascular bundle structure were selected as precursors. The porosity and conductive characteristics of 
the materials (ACK-x, x represents the activation temperature) were controllably adjusted by altering the KOH 
activation temperature. The findings suggest that the material ’ s notable expansion in SSA is linked to the rise in 
activation temperature. Notably, ACK-700 has a SSA of up to 2768 m

Waste bamboo fiber-based porous carbon was prepared from waste 
bamboo fiber as a carbon source after low-temperature carbonization 
with KOH as an activator. Then, the bamboo fiber-based porous carbon 
was characterized and assembled into a symmetric supercapacitor, 
which electrochemical performance was tested and the energy storage 
mechanism was analyzed.
1. Introduction
In view of the irreversible and progressive reduction of fossil fuels, 
developing renewable energy sources have emerged as effective strate -
gies to address the crisis of environmental damage and global warming. 
However, the key issue for the development of renewable energy is the 
availability of high efficiency, affordable and sustainable energy storage 
facilities [ 1 – 3 ]. Supercapacitors (SCs) stand out among other novel en -
ergy storage technologies owing to their affordability, fast responsive -
ness, superior power density, and simple operating environment [ 4 – 6 ]. 
SCs are prevalent utilized in sensors, industrial automation equipment ’ s 
auxiliary power supply, power grid energy storage devices, and new 
energy vehicle power systems [ 7 , 8 ]. On the basis of their energy storage 
techniques, SCs are grouped into pseudocapacitors using redox reactions 
and electrical double-layer capacitors (EDLCs) utilizing physical 
adsorption. Conductive polymers or metal oxides, which typically have 
inadequate cycling stability, are exemplary pseudocapacitors electrodes. 
Despite the fact that these materials increase the device ’ s energy den -
sity, chemical reactions cause the electrode material ’ s structure to 
deteriorate over time, leading to diminished cycling stability [ 9 ]. In 
contrast to pseudocapacitors, EDLCs employ excellently conductive 
carbon materials as electrodes. Among them, the most popular electrode 
material for EDLCs is porous carbon because of its rich pore structure, 
high conductivity, and extensive active specific surface area (SSA). 
These characteristics typically confer excellent capacitive performance 
and robust cycling stability [ 10 ].

of carbon materials [ 11 ]. Currently, majority of porous carbon is based 
on fossil fuels as precursors, which not only costly but also detrimental 
to the environment. Converting biomass into high-quality carbon-based 
electrode materials is of great relevance, particularly in the context of 
achieving “ dual carbon ” goals. Furthermore, biomass has evolved a 
natural spatial structure over hundreds of millions of years, which is 
crucial for energy storage. Biomass waste has become increasingly 
notable due to its renewable, environmentally friendly, and widely 
available sources, such as sargassum [ 12 ], bagasse [ 13 ], walnut shell 
[ 14 ], lotus flowers [ 15 ], and eggshells [ 16 ]. These materials offer 
promising potential for developing advanced energy storage technolo -
gies. It is estimated that biomass waste contributes approximately 10 % 
to the total global energy supply [ 17 ], and the total amount of exploit -
able biomass resources in China is currently equivalent to about 700 
million tons of standard coal. The utilization of waste biomass is not 
optimized in many developing countries due to differing levels of 
awareness about the circular economy and limitations in technological 
capabilities. Consequently, waste biomass is primarily disposed of 
through direct burning for heating, returning to fields, composting, or 
use as fodder. This singular approach to disposal not only results in low 
utilization rates but may also increase greenhouse gas emissions and 
contribute to environmental pollution. Converting it into superior per -
formance, potential porous carbon materials through suitable processes 
holds far-reaching significance for eco-environmental protection and 
sustainable energy development. This approach not only mitigates waste 
but also contributes to the development and implementation of green 
energy strategies.
Among the plethora of biomass waste resources, bamboo stands out 
as one of the fastest-growing plants globally. China, often referred to as 
the “ Kingdom of Bamboo ” , boasts the richest bamboo resources, the 
largest bamboo industry, and the most advanced processing and utili -
zation technologies in the world. During the processing of the bamboo 
industry, a significant amount of bamboo fiber waste is generated. These 
wastes are typically incinerated, leading not only to a squandering of 
resources but also to the emission of large quantities of pollutants such 
as carbon monoxide and dust. This results in severe environmental and 
atmospheric pollution. In fact, bamboo produces incredibly rich 
vascular bundle structures during its fast growth [ 18 ]. Furthermore, 
because of its abundant lignin component, bamboo is a superb precursor 
for carbon materials. Khuong et al. [ 19 ] successfully prepared porous 
carbon materials from bamboo and its solid residue after hydrothermal 
treatment as precursors, which were activated by carbon dioxide and 
showed good adsorption capacity when used as carbon dioxide adsor -
bents. Huang et al. [ 20 ] prepared bamboo-derived carbon-based com -
posites by one-step pyrolysis reaction, which showed excellent 
performance in the field of electromagnetic wave absorption. Yue et al. 
[ 21 ] prepared bamboo-based carbon materials by pre-oxidation and 
secondary carbonization, which exhibited an electrochemical capacity 
of 321 F/g in 6 M KOH electrolyte. Qiu et al. [ 22 ] investigated the role of 
cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin in bamboo chips on supercapacitor 
electrode materials using bamboo chips from a bamboo chopsticks 
processing plant as a carbon source. However, bamboo ’ s structural 
stability results in the retention of several cell wall remnants upon 
carbonization, which limited the material ’ s application in electrode 
materials by producing undeveloped pores, a low SSA, and suboptimal 
capacitance characteristics.
Researchers have developed a variety of synthesis methods to 
enhanced the capacitive properties of biomass carbon, such as activa -
tion, template method, hydrothermal method, molten salt method [ 23 ]. 
Among these methods, activation stands out as a traditional and efficient 
technique for generating porous carbon. Specifically, the original carbon 
skeleton of the biomass can be preserved while producing high-quality 
materials with rich porosity and appropriate distribution by carbon -
ization followed by chemical activation [ 24 ]. Among various chemical 
activation agents, KOH activation is particularly effective in producing 
materials with large SSA and well-distributed aperture, making it a 
widely used activator in the industry. Biomass porous carbon with a 
controllable pore structure can be obtained by carefully adjusting the 
parameters of KOH activation. Bag et al. [ 25 ] investigated the effects of 
KOH concentration and temperature on the properties of porous carbon 
derived from oak wood and prepared carbon materials with a surface 
area comparable to that of commercial activated carbon. Balasu -
bramanian et al. [ 26 ] produced porous carbon from banana leaves by 
adjusting the KOH activation temperature and used it as an electrode 
material for supercapacitors. At a current density of 0.3 A/g, the specific 
capacitance value could reach 391.3 F/g. Zheng et al. [ 27 ] regulated the 
pore structure of kapok flower-based porous carbon by changing the 
ratio of KOH to the precursor. The specific surface area of the porous 
carbon with the optimal ratio could reach 1904 m
2
/g, demonstrating 
excellent electrochemical performance.
In this study, porous carbon materials were generated using waste 
bamboo fibers from paper mills as precursors. Following temperature 
carbonization, the impact of KOH activation process on the micro- 
morphology, porosity, carbon microcrystal content, and electro -
chemical performances of the bamboo fiber-based porous carbon were 
examined. Finally, the material with optimal performance was assem -
bled into symmetric supercapacitors to assess its practical application 
potential. This study is significant in alleviating the problem of resource 
wastage of biomass waste and facilitating the advancement of superior 
supercapacitors.
2. Experiment
2.1. Materials
Waste bamboo fibers from the Anhui paper industry were selected 
for this study. The elemental composition of waste bamboo fibers is 
presented in Table S1 of the Supplementary Information. Sinopharm 
Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd provided the KOH and HCl (36 % – 38 %), 
which were used without additional purification. We bought acetylene 
black and polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) from Tianjin Avision Chemi -
cal Technology Co., Ltd.
2.2. Porous carbon preparation from bamboo fiber waste
Waste bamboo fiber-based porous carbon was prepared through a 
sequence of processes including pretreatment, temperature carboniza -
tion, and KOH activation. At first, deionized water was used to wash the 
waste bamboo fibers to get rid of any surface contaminants, then dried, 
and subsequently ground to a 100 mesh size using a crusher to obtain 
waste bamboo fiber powder. 5 g of waste bamboo fiber powder was 
placed in a porcelain boat and compacted. Then it was put into the 
center of a tube furnace. Under a nitrogen atmosphere with a flow rate of 
0.2 L/min, the temperature was progressively elevated from ambient 
temperature to 550 
◦
C at a heating rate of 5 
◦
C/min. This heating rate is 
designed to promote uniform and orderly pyrolysis of the sample, con -
trol the release rate of volatile matter, and lay the foundation for sub -
sequent activation [ 28 – 30 ]. After then, the temperature was kept at 
550 
◦
C for 2 h. This temperature can effectively reduce the loss of carbon 
content and improve the activation efficiency [ 31 , 32 ]. The carbonized 
waste bamboo fibers were collected once they had cooled to ambient 
temperature, and termed as PC, with a yield of approximately 22 %. To 
proceed with activation, 1 g of PC was ground and mixed with 4 g of 
KOH in a nickel boat. This mass ratio is based on the previous work of 
the research group and other studies that have been adopted and veri -
fied [ 33 – 35 ]. After that, the temperature was increased to the desig -
nated activation temperatures (600, 700, 800, 900 
◦
C) from ambient 
temperature under the same nitrogen atmosphere and held for an hour. 
The bamboo fiber-based porous carbon, known as ACK-x (where “ x" 
represents the activation temperature), was obtained by acid-washing it 
with 5 % HCl to get rid of any remaining alkali, then thoroughly rinsing 
it until it was neutral and drying it. Fig. 1 displays a flow chart that

2.4. Assembly of electrodes and symmetric supercapacitors
Acetylene black, polytetrafluoroethylene, and 4 mg of waste bamboo 
fiber-based porous carbon were combined in a 1:1:8 mass ratio to 
generate the precursor slurry. Then it was dispersed on nickel foam 
collector plate and compressed under a pressure of 10 MPa for 30 s. 
Subsequently, it was dried at 60 
◦
C overnight to form the working 
electrode.
2 mg of waste bamboo fiber-based porous carbon was mixed with the 
same reagent in the specified proportions and coated onto circular nickel 
foam. After pressing and drying, disc-shaped electrode plates were 
produced. Two electrode plates of equal mass were attached to the po -
larity. A separator is added between the polarities and a symmetric 
supercapacitor was obtained after assembly, which ensures balanced 
charge and discharge characteristics across both electrodes.

3. Results and discussion
3.1. Morphology and structure characteristics
Low-cost waste bamboo fibers served as the raw materials in this 
study. These fibers were processed through washing, drying, grinding, 
and carbonization at low temperatures, followed by activation with 
KOH. Subsequently, porous carbon materials based on waste bamboo 
fiber were produced by washing the material with hydrochloric acid and 
deionized water. Fig. 2 A presents a schematic diagram of the synthesis 
procedure for bamboo fiber-based porous carbon. Finally, the resulting 
porous carbon was made into electrodes to evaluate its performance in 
supercapacitors.

Fig. 2 B-E displays the SEM images of PC, ACK-600, ACK-700, and 
ACK-800. After carbonization, the bamboo fiber retains its original 
vascular bundle structure ( Fig. 2 B), which primarily functions as a sieve 
tube for the transport of water and nutrients in biomass materials. 
During high-temperature carbonization, cellulose, lignin, and other 
components undergo pyrolysis, exposing the natural pore structure of 
the biomass. This exposure is advantageous for full entry of the activator 
into the carbon matrix, thus achieving better activation.
Fig. 2 C-E depicts the sample morphologies following activation at 
various temperatures using KOH as the activator. A highly developed 
pore structure and a looser, more curled shape are the results of acti -
vation. The material is enriched with numerous micropores and meso -
pores at an activation temperature of 700 
◦
C, creating a three- 
dimensional, disordered, and interconnected pore structure. This 
transformation significantly increases the material ’ s SSA, enhances 
electrolyte diffusion, and reduces the migration distance of the elec -
trolyte, optimizing electrochemical performance. The etching impact of 
KOH on the material was further intensified with the increase in acti -
vation temperature. The intrinsic carbon skeleton of bamboo fibers may 
collapse and the pore structure may burst as a result of excessive etching. 
Carbon fragments will consequently occupy some of the pores, hinder -
ing the porous carbon material from making contact with the reactive 
substance, thereby impairing the conductivity of the material.
TEM was used to further analyze the microstructure of ACK-700, as 
seen in Fig. 2 F-G and Fig. S1 . ACK-700 primarily consists of disordered 
carbon and features abundant worm-like micropores, along with a small 
number of pseudo-graphite domains. These pseudo-graphite domains 
contribute to enhancing the material ’ s conductivity, while the well- 
developed pore structure provides ample space for charge storage, 
thus improving the material ’ s overall electrochemical performance. 
Therefore, the porous carbon material produced from bamboo fiber and 
activated at 700 
◦
C exhibits abundant pores, a dense and uniform dis -
tribution, and good electrical conductivity. These characteristics facili -
tates efficient charge transport by ensuring full contact between the 
material and the KOH solution. Consequently, this configuration allows 
for the attainment of excellent capacitive performance. Fig. S1 presents 
the elemental mapping of ACK-700, demonstrating that the material ’ s C, 
N and O are evenly and continuously dispersed throughout. This ho -
mogeneous distribution is crucial for improving the porous carbon 
material ’ s electrochemical performance and stability.

(DFT) approach was applied to examine the samples ’ porosity and pore 
size. The results are presented in Fig. 3 G and Table 1 , providing detailed 
insights into the pore sizes and distribution within the material, which 
are crucial for evaluating its effectiveness in applications requiring high 
surface area and pore accessibility. The porous carbon ’ s SSA, porosity, 
and pore size are all significantly impacted by the activation tempera -
ture. The material ’ s pore structure becomes more developed as the re -
action temperature climbs and the specific surface area increases. 
Micropores are the “ shortcut ” to enhancing SSA. Materials rich in mi -
cropores usually exhibit extremely high SSA. The presence of mesopores 
can increase SSA, but the efficiency is lower than that of micropores 
[ 55 ]. However, the percentage of micropores significantly reduces and 
the average pore size grows when the activation temperature exceeds 
700 
◦
C. This change is attributed to the activator ’ s reactive ions getting 
more embedded in the carbon matrix at higher temperatures, resulting 
in an enhanced etching effect. Some micropores are destroyed as a result 
of this process, which subsequently interconnect to form larger meso -
pores, thereby increasing the mesopore volume, the total pore volume, 
and the specific surface area of the sample [ 56 ]. Notably, ACK-700 ex -
hibits the highest percentage of micropores along with a moderate 
amount of mesopores. This balanced pore structure helps to improve 
capacity, rate capability, and cycle stability of supercapacitors. The 
presence of micropores allows for high capacitance through increased 
surface area interaction with electrolytes, while the mesopores facilitate 
rapid ion transport, essential for accomplishing superior rate capability 
and durability in energy storage equipment [ 57 ].
The surface elemental composition of the material, specifically ACK- 
700, was analyzed using XPS, the results displayed in Fig. 3 H-I, Fig. S2
and Table 2 . The two prominent peaks of the spectra located at about 
285.1 eV and 532.4 eV are C 1 s and O 1 s, respectively ( Fig. S2 ). 
Additionally, a weak peak at 402 eV represent to N 1 s, showcasing the 
presence of nitrogen. The elemental analysis of ACK-700 indicates a 
composition of 82.9 % carbon, 15.7 % oxygen, and 0.2 % nitrogen, 
highlighting a carbon-rich material with minor contributions from ox -
ygen and nitrogen ( Table 2 ). This composition suggests potential func -
tionalities that can augment the electrochemical capabilities of the 
device. The C 1 s domain of ACK-700 was analyzed and decomposed into 
four distinct component peaks ( Fig. 3 H), which correspond to different 
carbon bonding environments: C-Si (282.5 eV), C-C (284.2 eV), C-O 
(286.1 eV), and C = O (288.1 eV). Additionally, the O 1 s domain was 
decomposed into three independent component peaks representing 
various oxygen-related functionalities ( Fig. 3 I): OH (529.6 eV), C = O 
(531.2 eV), and C-O (532.7 eV). These oxygenic groups are essential as 
they enhance the wettability of the material within the electrolyte, 
thereby improving ionic conductivity and providing pseudocapacitance, 
which contributes to the overall energy storage capacity of the super -
capacitors [ 58 ].
3.2. Electrochemical property analysis
A three-electrode device was adopted for measuring the electro -
chemical performances of alkali-activated bamboo fiber-based porous 
carbon material. All four samples ’ CV curves showed rectangle-like 
forms when scanned at the scanning speed of 5 mV s
� 1 
( Fig. 4 A). This 
shape is characteristic of EDLCs, indicating that the predominantly 
source of the capacitive behavior is the charge separation at the 
electrode-solution interface, rather than faradaic reactions. This typical 
behavior highlights the materials ’ effective charge storage mechanism, 
which is crucial for high-performance supercapacitors. The ACK-700 
sample ’ s CV curve exhibits the biggest enclosed area among the evalu -
ated samples, suggesting that it possesses the greatest mass-specific 
capacitance. This suggests that ACK-700 provides superior energy 
storage capacity over other samples, likely ascribed to its surface 
chemistry and optimal pore structure, which enhance electrical con -
ductivity and electrolyte ion accessibility within the electrode material 
[ 59 ]. Moreover, ACK-700 displays a weak redox peak from � 0.8 ~ � 0.4 
V, ascribed to the material ’ s abundance of oxygenic groups. These 
groups enhance the wettability of the material, thus optimizing its 
capacitive properties.
Fig. 4 B presents the GCD graphs (at 0.5 A g
� 1 
current density) for the 
four porous carbons. All samples exhibit symmetrical triangle features

4. Conclusion
In summary, waste bamboo fibers were successfully converted into 
bamboo fiber-based porous carbon materials with an exceedingly SSA, 
an optimized pore size distribution, and exceptional electrical conduc -
tivity using a straightforward and efficient carbonization and activation 
procedure. For natural plant cells to preserve their distinctive and sturdy 
skeleton, carbonization is crucial. KOH activation produces inter -
connected micropores and mesopores within the framework. Addition -
ally, the electrochemical property of the bamboo fiber-based carbon 
material is improved by the plentiful oxygenic groups. In a three-
